toc.title: Essential one: the biological states of the body
Essential two: the states are unconscious

sections.title: You can't choose it, but you can curate for it
It's not about hacking the vagus nerve

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory is very complex. If you're a complete and utter beginner, having a foundation can help you move on to learning more in depth. Here are what I think are the three essentials:

ol: The biological states of the body.

blocks.p: You might sense a theme in all three.

The theory is especially complex if you start with the primary source. Dr. Porges' book The Polyvagal Theory is not an easy read. The Pocket Guide to the Polyvagal Theory is much more digestible. That's actually where I went to really get it, and then I went back to The Polyvagal Theory, his first book.

blocks.h: Essential one: the biological states of the body

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory is inherently about mammals. It touches on other animals, but the focus is really on mammals. And mammals can be said to be in, basically, and I say this in italics, basically one of three states.
If you're a polyvagal nerd, I know. I get it. It's more complex than that, of course. But basically one of three states, so calm down.
These three states are a result of the body detecting safety or danger in the environment, and each has specific biological pathways responsible for it:

ul: Safety and social engagement. This is where we're safe, and we can socially engage with others. We can smile. We can use something called vocal prosody. We can make gentle eye contact. We can hug.

Flight/fight mobility. It's what it sounds like. This is the biology responsible for mobilization. When the mammal is in danger, it mobilizes, running away or being aggressive, to get out of the danger.

Shutdown immobility. These pathways are responsible for the body immobilizing in the face of extreme life threat. The mammal may be dying, or perceives or detects that it's dying, so it goes into a shutdown state where it immobilizes and kind of plays dead.

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory basically says that if one of these states is active, you don't have access to the others. Again, I know I'm talking in very black-and-white, cartoony, one-dimensional terms. That's the basic idea.
If you're in a flight/fight state, your capacity to socially engage is way, way less. If you're in a shutdown, immobilized state, your capacity to mobilize, to fight or run, is way, way less.

So if you exist in one of the defensive states, flight, fight, or shutdown, all of these become a lot more difficult: socially engaging, connecting with others, being present, being calm, being relaxed, being self-reflective, immobilizing and going to sleep in peace, sitting in class and paying attention, focusing. That's because the safety pathways aren't active, and they're very important for all of those things and a lot more.

blocks.h: Essential two: the states are unconscious

blocks.p: These biological states of the body are unconscious. That means you don't choose your biological state. You don't choose to be in safe and social, flight/fight, or shutdown.

These are responses to the environment, and also to the internal world, but let's focus on the environment. Your body gets inputs from your five senses, and then your brain stem basically decides whether it's safe, dangerous, or life threat. Then it shifts the body into one of the defensive states, or the safe state, to survive or to optimize its resources.

All three of these states evolved within us to increase the chances of survival. Running away or fighting increases your chances of survival in the face of danger. Playing dead increases your chances of survival in the face of life threat, because you can come out of it when you have the capacity, or the moment, to do so. And the safety state optimizes your bodily resources for health, growth, and restoration, as Dr. Porges so often says. All three are there to enhance the body's well-being, or to make sure it survives whatever situation it's in.

blocks.h3: You can't choose it, but you can curate for it

blocks.p: So you cannot choose your polyvagal state. But you can increase the chances of being in your safety state.

ul: Your environment. The five senses are what bring in cues of safety or danger. If you can shape your environment to increase the cues of safety coming into your system, you probably have more of a chance of being in your safety state. These are called passive safety cues: adjusting the lighting in your space, putting comforting things on your wall, putting on music, or maybe having no sound, smells. Things that feel good or comforting, or that you just like.

Safe people. Good relationships and friendships, shared relationships, empathy, understanding. If you have those with others in your life, that's really going to boost your chances of being in your safety state.
Things you actively do. Hobbies, creativity, athletics, yoga, dancing, swimming. Taking part in those further increases your chances of activating your safety state.

blocks.p: It's not like you just choose to be in your safe and social state. You really have to curate your life to increase the chances of being there.

blocks.h3: It's not about hacking the vagus nerve

blocks.p: No, it's not as easy as resetting or hacking or activating your vagus nerve. That's really a misunderstanding of the theory, but these ideas are out there, and honestly, they're pretty rampant. When you see them, I'd take it as a red flag that the person doesn't quite get the theory.

The focus of the Polyvagal Theory, oddly, is not really the vagus nerve itself. Of course it's a big part of the theory, but the vagus nerve is really just a highway the messages are sent through. So stimulating or activating the vagus nerve is not the point.

Plus, if that's the way you think, you're not really being with your direct, felt experience, and that's way more important. If you're trying to activate or hack, you're trying to get rid of something. When it comes to trauma relief and mindfulness, it's not about getting rid of it. It's about inviting it, and being able to tolerate and experience whatever you have inside of you.
So no one is choosing to be in or out of these states. That's not how it works. But you can increase the chances of being in your safety state by shaping your environment and curating your life.

The Polyvagal Theory does directly connect to pretty much every aspect of our experience: our thoughts, our feelings, our internal sensations, our behaviors, our relationships. But it's biology first, and then those things.

The Polyvagal Theory is a unifying theory. It doesn't look at these things as silos that exist on their own. It says biology is primary, and it influences everything else. The polyvagal state shift happens first: safe and social, flight, fight, or shutdown. Then, depending on the state you're in, your thoughts change, your feelings change, your internal sensations change, and how you interact with people changes. The polyvagal state is the primary factor.
Think of it like dominoes falling. You knock over one domino, it knocks over the next, which knocks over the next.

The first domino is the polyvagal state. Say your body shifts into a flight or fight state. After the biology shifts, your feelings change, and you might feel more aggressive or angry. Then, or maybe along with that, your cognitions change, and your thoughts become more blaming or shaming or judging. Then the way you relate to other people changes, and you might be outwardly more blaming or aggressive. Then they react to that and give you some energy back, and you feel that.

And even before the first domino falls, the state shift was triggered by something in the environment. Maybe the lights went off all of a sudden, and now you feel anxious. Now you have anxious feelings, and thoughts like, "Oh my gosh, what's going on? Someone's out to get me." That changes the energy you bring and your tenseness. Someone else feels that, and they adjust along with it. Now they're panicking and you're panicking. You get the idea.
As far as the Polyvagal Theory is concerned, the state shift is the catalyst for the other domains of your life: your thoughts, your feelings, your sensations, your relationships, and on and on.

I see a lot of people in the polyvagal and trauma sphere talking about trauma responses, but on more of a behavioral level: "When this happened, this is how I reacted," or "Now, this is how I still act." The problem is they're focusing on the action. That's absolutely important. But the trauma response stems from a polyvagal state. Focusing only on trauma responses misses a big part of the picture.
So, to sum up the third essential: it's biology first, and the other stuff follows.

Some of you are seasoned polyvagal nerds. I think it's always good to come back to the basics and ask ourselves: What do I know here, and what does it mean to me now? If I could sum it up, how would I do that? This is my attempt. These are what I think are the three absolute essentials of the Polyvagal Theory.
